card: Paper card. Question: How does the machinability of Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy compare to 304 stainless steel in terms of cutting forces, tool wear, surface quality, and microstructural changes during milling?. System: Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) and X5CrNi18-10 (304) stainless steel. Processing: Face milling using a 12 mm diameter shank cutter with two indexable carbide inserts (grade HSC 05, PVTi coating) on a FIRST MCV 300 vertical milling center; dry cutting conditions; 25 tests using Taguchi method with cutting speed (vc), feed per tooth (fz), and axial depth of cut (ap) varied; radial depth of cut ae = 12 mm (100%); sample dimensions 145 × 15 × 6 mm³ for HEA. Test conditions: Dry cutting; spindle speeds up to 8000 rpm; feed rates up to 103 mm/min; axial depth of cut (ap) ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.42 mm; feed per tooth (fz) ranging from 0.05 mm/tooth to 0.15 mm/tooth; cutting speed (vc) varied across 5 levels; temperature measured via thermo vision camera (0–500 °C range); cutting forces measured with Kistler 9257B dynamometer. Findings: The machinability of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of 304 stainless steel based on the resultant cutting force.; Cutting temperatures ranged from 120 °C to 281 °C, with the maximum temperature (213.2 °C) recorded after about 6 s of processing.; The axial depth of cut (ap) was identified as the main influencing parameter on cutting temperature, with maximum temperatures (240–281 °C) occurring at ap = 0.42 mm.; Maximum flank wear width (VBB max) was 86 µm for the first cutting edge (CE1) and 67 µm for the second cutting edge (CE2).; Maximum crater dimensions on the rack face for CE2 were KBmax = 490 µm and KMmax = 225 µm.; Surface roughness values ranged from 0.39 µm to 2.058 µm, with the best values obtained at minimum feed (fz = 0.05 mm/tooth).; Microhardness of the machined HEA surfaces ranged from 365 HV0.2 to 444 HV0.2, attributed to material inhomogeneity and self-hardening.; XRD analysis showed that patterns for as-cast and machined surfaces were very similar, with no new phases formed during machining.. Mechanism: The superior machinability of the HEA compared to stainless steel is attributed to its specific cutting force behavior, where the resultant force is lower despite higher hardness. The irregular chip fragmentation and surface defects are caused by the inhomogeneity of the cast material and the presence of hard intermetallic phases (e.g., Fe2Al5, FeAl3) which act as micro-edges causing tool wear. Self-hardening effects and oxidation during cutting contribute to the increased microhardness and chip fragmentation, while the similar XRD patterns indicate the material withstands heating cycles without phase transformation.. Limitations: The study was limited to dry cutting conditions and did not evaluate the effects of cooling and lubrication. The research is described as preliminary, and the number of reference XRD patterns available in the database is limited. The study did not cover extended ranges of cutting parameters for finish and rough cuts, nor did it generate predictive mathematical models for material removal rate or tool life.. Future work: More detailed research should be achieved to have a more precise image of the machinability of the HEA by considering the cutting speed, material removal rate and cutting tool life. Furthermore, extended ranges of the cutting parameters should be considered for both finish cut and rough cut and to generate predictive mathematical models to improve processing and optimize cutting parameters.. Quote: "In terms of cutting forces, the behavior of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of stainless steel."

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

card: Paper card. Question: How can process parameters be optimized to minimize and align surface roughness (Ra and Rz) on curvilinear titanium alloy surfaces regardless of the surface shape and tilted angle?. System: Ti6Al4V titanium alloy (annealed at 750 °C). Processing: Turning of spherical curvilinear surfaces (radius of curvature R = 14 mm, length L = 10 mm) using a CNC machine with interpolated axes, sintered carbide insert (N123F1–0318–R0S05F), cutting edge radius rε = 1.588 mm, and variable feed rates (f) and cutting speeds (vc). Test conditions: Tilted surface angles δ ranging from ±17° to 0°; feed rates varied across 3 levels; cutting speed varied across 3 levels; depth of cut ap = 0.7 mm (case study); measurement via Talysurf Intra 50 profilometer (ISO 4287/ISO25178 standards). Findings: Cutting speed has an insignificant effect on surface roughness parameters (p = 0.531 for Ra and p = 0.355 for Rz).; Feed rate and tilted surface angle are the most influential parameters on surface roughness (Ra and Rz).; The optimized method achieved surface roughness parameters below upper limits (Ra ≤ 0.63 μm and Rz ≤ 3.2 μm) across the full range of tilted angles.; Machining time with optimized feed rate was 160 s, compared to 304 s required for a constant minimum feed rate (fmin = 0.03 mm/rev) to achieve the same roughness alignment.; The optimized feed rate range was 0.03–0.115 mm/rev, whereas a constant feed rate of 0.085 mm/rev only yielded acceptable roughness for tilted angles between −1° and 12°.; The regression equations for roughness prediction were simplified to depend only on feed rate and tilted angle due to the lack of cutting speed effect.. Mechanism: The authors explain that during turning of curvilinear surfaces, the change in the undeformed chip area shape and the modification of angles between the cutting insert flank face and the work surface cause variable surface roughness. By approximating the curved contour with elementary straight lines and developing regression models based on experimental data, they can calculate specific feed rates for each surface segment to maintain aligned roughness values.. Limitations: The study notes that the proposed method relies on a simplification of approximating curved contour sections by elementary straight lines, though geometrical analysis confirmed the insignificant effect of this simplification on the contour shape and undeformed chip area. Additionally, the current model does not account for cutting depth, radius of surface curvature, tool wear, or total cutting force components.. Future work: The authors plan to modify the proposed method to apply a new calculation method based on a neural network to provide more accurate prediction of surface roughness parameters and to include the impact of additional cutting data such as cutting depth, radius of surface curvature, tool wear, and total cutting force components.. Quote: "The results analysis of the experiment showed the significant effect of the feed rate f and the tilted angle of surface δ on the surface roughness."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the microstructure, phase formation, and corrosion properties of AlCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy coatings differ when prepared by high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) versus high-velocity air fuel (HVAF) thermal spraying?. System: Equimolar AlCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (feedstock produced by inert gas atomization). Processing: Thermal spraying using HVOF (K2 liquid-fueled system) and HVAF (M3TM-HVAF system with 4L4C nozzle, 250 mm length, 22.75 mm exit diameter) on mild steel substrates (EN 1.0045) grit blasted at 2.5 bar, 70° angle; HVOF used -45 +15 µm powder, HVAF used -33 +15 µm powder. Test conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in 0.5 M NaCl and 0.05 M H2SO4 aerated electrolytes at room temperature; surface interrupted at 2 mA/cm2 for microscopy; microhardness HV 0.1; roughness Ra, Rz; porosity via optical microscopy. Findings: Porosity reduced from 0.6 ± 0.2% in HVOF coatings to 0.3 ± 0.1% in HVAF coatings; Microhardness increased from 600 ± 50 HV 0.1 (HVOF) to 680 ± 20 HV 0.1 (HVAF); Surface roughness decreased from Ra: 4.6 ± 0.1 µm (HVOF) to Ra: 4.0 ± 0.2 µm (HVAF); Corrosion current density (icorr) reduced by a factor of two in HVAF coatings compared to HVOF in NaCl electrolyte; Passivation current density in H2SO4 reduced to 0.013 mA/cm2 for HVAF vs. 0.073 mA/cm2 for HVOF; Pitting potential remained similar for both coatings (947 mV for HVOF vs. 957 mV for HVAF); No distinct oxide lamellae formed in HVAF coatings due to reduced thermal input; Metastable bcc (B2) structure retained in both coating types with lattice parameter a = 2.87 Å. Mechanism: The reduced thermal input in HVAF spraying suppresses oxygen pick-up and oxide formation, leading to lower porosity and a denser microstructure. The finer powder fraction used in HVAF results in decreased grain size and increased hardness. The improved corrosion resistance and passivation behavior in HVAF coatings are attributed to the formation of a denser and more protective passive layer, likely due to the reduced structural defects and lower oxide content.. Future work: The authors state that the HVAF process shows high potential for processing HEAs and imply further investigation into optimizing parameters for even better defect reduction and corrosion resistance, though specific future experiments are not detailed beyond the general potential of the process.. W2754629136.title: Microstructure and Wear Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiTi High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Produced by HVOF

card: Paper card. Question: What is the influence of titanium content (molar ratios x = 0.0 to 1.5) on the microstructure, phase formation, and wear behavior of the AlCoCrFeNiTix high-entropy alloy system?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTix with molar ratios x = 0.0; 0.2; 0.5; 0.8; 1.0; 1.5. Processing: Arc-melting of elemental granules (≥99.9% purity) in a water-cooled copper crucible under argon atmosphere (1.1 bar, 2 × 10−4 mbar base pressure), remelted three times with turning for homogeneity; cooling rate <50 K/s. Test conditions: Microhardness (HV0.5, 10 indents), XRD (Co Kα, 20°–130° 2θ), DSC (1800 K to room temperature, 20 K/min cooling), ball-on-disk, oscillating wear, and scratch tests; reference material: bearing steel EN 1.3505. Findings: The alloy without titanium (x = 0.0) exhibits a homogeneous microstructure with a single chemically ordered bcc (B2) phase and an average microhardness of 550 HV0.5.; Alloying with titanium causes the formation of two major bcc phases (ordered B2 and disordered A2) and increases microstructural heterogeneity.; For x ≥ 0.5, a minor face-centred cubic (fcc) phase forms in the cell walls, and for x = 0.8, a tetragonal σ phase is detected.; Microhardness increases with titanium content, reaching a maximum of 770 HV0.5 for the equimolar composition (x = 1.0), then decreases to 730 HV0.5 for x = 1.5 due to porosity.; The alloy AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 shows superior wear resistance in ball-on-disk tests with the lowest wear depth compared to other compositions and bearing steel.; Under oscillating wear conditions, the alloy with x = 0.5 has the lowest wear depth, but all HEAs exhibit higher wear depth (lower resistance) than the bearing steel.; Samples with x ≥ 0.8 exhibit spalling and secondary cracks under abrasive conditions due to the formation of complex phases (tetragonal, cc, hexagonal Laves) that reduce ductility.. Mechanism: Titanium's large atomic radius causes solid solution strengthening and shifts lattice parameters, while its addition stabilizes a second disordered bcc phase and promotes the formation of complex intermetallic phases (fcc, σ, cc, Laves) at higher concentrations. These complex phases increase hardness but reduce ductility by possessing low numbers of slip systems, leading to brittle behavior and spalling under abrasive loads.. Limitations: The authors note that the formation of the σ phase is sensitive to manufacturing conditions and can be dissolved by heat treatment. Additionally, for the highest titanium content (x = 1.5), cavities and shrinkage porosity caused by different phase contraction reduced microhardness and may have influenced wear results.. Future work: The authors propose that AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 is a promising candidate for wear protection applications in both bulk and coating materials, suggesting further investigation into its potential for such uses.. Quote: "Alloying with titanium showed strong influence on the resulting microstructure and lead to an increase of microstructural heterogeneity."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the power of atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) influence the microstructure, frictional wear resistance, and corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings?. System: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings (HEACs) on low carbon steel (45#) substrates. Processing: Atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using mechanically milled powders (15–50 μm) with four power levels (H1 < H2 < H3 < H4); H4 utilized the highest hydrogen-gas flow rate and power. Test conditions: Tribological tests: Si3N4 ball (5 mm), 5 N load, 1200 s sliding time; Corrosion tests: 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, room temperature, 240 h immersion, potentiodynamic polarization, EIS (100 kHz–10 MHz). Findings: Volume fractions of pores decreased from 4.31 ± 0.90% (H1) to 0.59 ± 0.12% (H4) as APS power increased.; The H4 coating achieved the lowest coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.38 ± 0.08, indicating the best wear resistance.; H4 coating exhibited the highest corrosion potential and lowest corrosion current density among all samples.; Impedance modulus |Z| at 0.1 Hz for H4 was ~1459 Ω·cm², significantly higher than H1 (~382 Ω·cm²).; The H4 coating thickness was 80 ± 8 μm, showing significantly higher deposition efficiency than H1 (56 ± 6 μm).; Oxygen content in wear trace regions (delamination, debris, etc.) for H4 ranged from 14.27 to 20.22 at. %.; The passive film on H4 contained bound water (H2O) at 532.5 eV, which helps assemble dissolving metal ions.. Mechanism: Increased APS power enhances the melting rate and alloying process, reducing porosity and improving coating density. During wear, multi-component metal oxides form and flake off to create a lubricating layer that prevents severe adhesion wear. For corrosion, the dense microstructure and the presence of bound water in the passive film (composed of Cr/Fe oxides) enhance protection against pitting initiation by Cl− ions.. Limitations: The text notes that excessive gas flow in intermediate power settings (H1-H3) caused rapid cooling, leading to uneven melting and high porosity; also, the H4 coating still exhibited some pitting corrosion at phase boundaries after 240 h immersion.. Future work: The authors state that by changing processing parameters, it is feasible to acquire an AlCoCrFeNi HEAC with both excellent wear resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance, implying further optimization of APS parameters is viable.. Quote: "The frictional wear and corrosion resistance of the coating are simultaneously improved with an increase of the power of APS."

W3115106890.title: Microstructure and Wear Behavior of the High‐Velocity‐Oxygen‐Fuel Sprayed and Spark Plasma Sintered High‐Entropy Alloy AlCrFeCoNi

card: Paper card. Question: How do the synthesis methods and operating temperatures influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and tribological performance (friction and wear) of high-entropy coatings (HECs) in various industrial applications?. System: High-entropy coatings (HECs) including metallic (e.g., CuMoTaWV, FeCoCrNiMo0.2, AlCrTiV), ceramic (e.g., (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N, TiVCrZrWNx), and composite systems; base elements include Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Al, Ti, V, Mo, W, Ta, Nb, Zr, Si, Cu, Mn.. Processing: Fabrication via vapor deposition (magnetron sputtering, reactive sputtering, vacuum arc), thermal spraying (atmospheric plasma spray (APS), high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF)), and cladding (laser, plasma). Key parameters include substrate bias voltage (0 to -200 V), nitrogen flow rate (FN), substrate temperature (300 °C), annealing (300 °C), and feedstock preparation (mechanical alloying, gas atomization).. Test conditions: Tribological testing performed using ball-on-disk and pin-on-disk setups against counterfaces of Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15). Tests conducted from room temperature (RT) up to 600 °C, varying sliding speeds, loads, and sliding distances.. Findings: The CuMoTaWV coating exhibited adaptive tribological behavior: lowest coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rate at RT due to Ta- and W-rich tribo-layers; galling wear at 200 °C; reduced wear at 400 °C due to adaptive CuO formation; and low COF but slightly higher wear at 600 °C due to excessive V-rich phase oxidation.; In (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N coatings, increasing substrate bias from 0 V to -200 V increased hardness from 28.2 GPa to 34.5 GPa and reduced wear rate to 1.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m at -100 V, attributed to grain boundary strengthening and denser structure.; The (AlCrTiVZr)N film deposited at a nitrogen flow of 12 sccm achieved super-hardness of 41.8 GPa and a low wear rate of 2.3 × 10−7 mm3/N.m.; The FeCoCrNiMo0.2 coating fabricated via APS showed a volume wear rate of 3.9 × 10−5 mm3/N.m, significantly lower than the HVOF coating (4.8 × 10−4 mm3/N.m) and the substrate (5.4 × 10−4 mm3/N.m).; TiVCrZrWNx coatings formed a self-lubricating V2O5 phase during rolling friction, reducing the friction coefficient to 0.38.; The (CrNbSiTiZr)C film exhibited a minimum friction coefficient of 0.3 and a wear rate of 4.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m due to the formation of a transfer film and high H/E (0.151) and H3/E2 (0.747) ratios.; Annealing the CuMoTaWV film at 300 °C improved its adhesion and wear resistance at both room temperature and 300 °C compared to the as-deposited state.. Mechanism: Tribological improvements are attributed to the formation of self-lubricating oxide layers (e.g., CuO, MoO3, V2O5) at elevated temperatures, the high hardness and nano-crystalline grain structure of the coatings, the presence of secondary phases (e.g., V-rich zones), and the balance between hardness and toughness enhanced by substrate bias or plasma nitriding. Wear mechanisms vary from adhesive wear and galling at intermediate temperatures to mild abrasive wear and oxidative wear at higher temperatures.. Limitations: The text notes that results from different wear experiments using different tools and parameters may not be directly comparable. It also highlights that there is very limited information available regarding high-entropy coatings developed by vapor deposition and cold spray methods compared to thermal spraying and cladding.. Future work: The authors state that further investigation is needed to optimize process parameters, explore more manufacturing processes (especially for HEA wires and targets), and conduct more extensive and interdisciplinary tribological investigations at high temperatures to better understand the complex wear-related phenomena.. Quote: "At RT, the lowest COF and wear rate was observed due to the formation of the Ta- and W-rich tribo layer in the wear track."

Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Silver (Ag) and the variation in temperature affect the tribological properties and wear mechanisms of plasma-sprayed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-based high-entropy coatings?. System: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-Ag (HEA-Ag) and Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti (HEC) coatings formed on carbon steel. Processing: Plasma spraying. Test conditions: Temperature range from 25 to 750 °C; ball-on-disk sliding; counterface not explicitly named in the specific Li et al. summary but implied standard tribological testing. Findings: At high temperatures (600–750 °C), the HEA-Ag coating achieved a friction coefficient of 0.253 and a wear rate of 0.89 × 10−5 mm3/N.m at 750 °C.; The wear rate of both HEA and HEA + Ag coatings was significantly lower than that of tool steels SKH 51 and Q 125 at all test temperatures.; At low temperatures (RT to 400 °C), tribological properties depended on mechanical properties and Ag lubrication.; The addition of Ag had little effect on the friction coefficient at high temperatures.; The as-sprayed coatings comprised a major FCC solid solution with minor BCC phase.; A lubricious film consisting of Ag and various oxides formed on the frictional surface.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the outstanding tribological properties at high temperatures to the formation of a lubricious film on the frictional surface consisting of Ag and various oxides, which contributes to low friction and wear. At low temperatures, the properties are governed by the mechanical properties of the coating and the solid lubrication provided by Ag.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations for this specific study, only that the study investigated the effect of Ag addition and temperature.. card: Paper card. Question: What are the microstructure evolution, microhardness, and corrosion behavior of (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy alloy coatings fabricated by plasma spraying on Q235 steel substrates?. System: (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy alloy coating on Q235 steel substrate. Processing: Vacuum plasma spraying (ZP-2000, DWAUTO) using atomized powder; arc power 30 kW, current 500 A, Ar flow 45 L/min, powder delivery gas 4 L/min, spraying distance 100 mm. Test conditions: Microhardness tested at 500 g load for 15 s; electrochemical polarization in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 298 K, potential range −0.5 to 0.5 V, scan rate 1 mV/s. Findings: A new Laves phase formed in the coating compared to the powder, which contained only a simple FCC phase.; Elemental segregation occurred with Cr and Nb enriched in the interdendritic phase, while Co, Fe, and Ni concentrated in the dendritic region.; The transition zone width at the coating-substrate junction was merely 2 μm.; The microhardness of the coating was 321 HV0.5, significantly higher than the substrate's ~122 HV0.5.; The coating exhibited a significantly higher pitting potential and lower passivation current density than other HEA coatings in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.; Selective corrosion occurred where the interdendritic phase rich in Nb and Cr was preferentially corroded as an anode.; Tiny dish-shaped pitting pits with diameters of 1~5 μm were observed only in the gray (interdendritic) phase region.. Mechanism: The formation of the Laves phase and elemental segregation is attributed to the faster cooling rate of plasma spraying and differences in melting points (Cr: 2133 K, Nb: 2750 K vs. Co: 1770 K, Fe: 1811 K, Ni: 1728 K). The excellent corrosion resistance is due to a dense passivation film containing Cr2O3 and Nb2O5, while selective corrosion occurs because the standard potential of Nb (−1.1 V) and Cr (−0.74 V) is more negative than Fe, Ni, and Co, causing the Cr/Nb-rich interdendritic phase to act as an anode once the film is damaged.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The width of transition zone was merely 2 μm."

Question: Can an Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating be successfully fabricated on an AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate via laser cladding to improve its wear and corrosion resistance, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. Processing: Laser cladding using a TR050 type CO2 high-power laser under 99.999% argon protection; mixed powders ball milled, preset with 4 vol % PVA solution (0.6 mm thickness); laser power 3000 W, scanning speed 10 mm/s, spot diameter 4 mm, overlap rate 25%. Test conditions: Dry sliding wear: 98 N load, 0.4187 m/s speed, 75 mins duration (1884 m distance), bearing steel (AISI52100) friction pair; Corrosion: potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt % NaCl solution, −2.5 V to 1.5 V range, 1 mV/s scan rate; Microhardness: 100 g load, 15 s dwell time. Findings: The coating consists of a simple FCC solid solution phase with fine dendritic microstructure.; Microhardness of the coating is HV0.1365, approximately 3.7 times higher than the AZ91D matrix (HV0.198).; The coating's wear weight loss is about 2.5 times smaller than that of the AZ91D matrix.; Wear rate of the coating is 11.93 μg/s compared to 30.38 μg/s for the AZ91D matrix.; The coating exhibits abrasive wear, whereas the AZ91D matrix exhibits adhesive wear.; Corrosion potential (Ecorr) of the coating is −0.998 V, significantly more positive than the AZ91D matrix (−1.46 V).; Corrosion current density (icorr) of the coating is 1.60 × 10−4 A/cm2, lower than the AZ91D matrix (6.20 × 10−4 A/cm2).; Copper segregates significantly in the inter-dendrite regions due to positive mixing enthalpies with other elements.. Mechanism: The high microhardness and wear resistance are attributed to solid solution strengthening and fine grain strengthening from the rapid solidification process, combined with the alloy's superior work-hardening capacity which allows the coating to shear off steel debris that then acts as abrasive particles. The improved corrosion resistance is attributed to the formation of dense chromium, aluminum, and nickel oxides on the surface, which protect against the aggressive attack that occurs on the loose, porous magnesium oxide film of the AZ91D substrate.. Limitations: The authors state that the specific Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi composition selected is not superior to other high-entropy compositions and was chosen only for its known good corrosion resistance; they also note that obtaining high-quality laser-clad coatings on magnesium alloys is difficult due to the substrate's low melting and boiling points.. Future work: The authors propose that future selection of high-entropy alloy compositions for laser cladding should be based on whether the same alloy prepared by arc melting exhibits excellent corrosion performance; if so, it is a candidate, otherwise it should not be selected.. Quote: "The coating was composed of a simple FCC solid solution phase with a microhardness about 3.7 times higher than that of the AZ91D matrix."

W4220727698.title: Microstructural and Tribological Behavior of Thermal Spray CrMnFeCoNi High Entropy Alloy Coatings

card: Paper card. Question: How do crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC), temperature, and alloying elements influence the dry sliding wear rate, hardness, and coefficient of friction of high-entropy alloys?. System: Ingot cast high-entropy alloys including the Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi) and its variations (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiTiAl, CoCrFeNiCu, CoCrFeNiS), categorized by FCC, BCC, and dual-phase (FCC+BCC) crystal structures.. Processing: Manufacturing methods include arc melting (most common), vacuum arc melting, induction melting, and spark plasma sintering (SPS); ingots are remelted multiple times for homogeneity, and composites are prepared by mixing powders (e.g., with MoS2, graphite, Ag) before sintering.. Test conditions: Dry sliding conditions using ball-on-disk, pin-on-disk, and ball-on-block setups; counter bodies include Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15); tests conducted at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 600°C and beyond); loads and sliding velocities varied (e.g., 5 N, 0.28 m/s).. Findings: HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC+BCC alloys due to reduced ductility and limited slip systems.; The addition of Al and Ti to the Cantor alloy increased hardness by up to 40% and promoted a transition from FCC to harder BCC phases.; Wear rates for most HEAs decreased after reaching a certain elevated temperature due to the formation of a protective oxide layer at the sliding interface.; The addition of 0.2 to 1 at.% Cu to CoCrFeNi HEA reduced the wear rate at 600°C by 40–45% due to the lubricating nature of Cu at high temperatures.; Self-lubricating composites with MoS2 and graphite showed significantly lower coefficients of friction but higher wear rates above 200°C compared to the base SPSed HEA.; FCC phase HEAs exhibited higher coefficients of friction and lower hardness compared to BCC phase HEAs, resulting in larger wear tracks.; The addition of V increased hardness but subsequently increased the wear rate after a certain percentage was added.. Mechanism: The superior wear resistance of BCC phases is attributed to limited slip systems causing strong but brittle behavior. At elevated temperatures, wear reduction is driven by the formation of a protective oxide layer (tribo-oxidation) or self-lubricating phases (e.g., CrxSy, sheared Cu) that reduce friction and protect the surface. The 'cocktail effect' and lattice distortion contribute to solid solution strengthening and high hardness.. Limitations: The review notes that intrinsic brittleness in BCC alloys is a trade-off for wear resistance. The oxidation mechanisms are complex due to multiple elements, and the influence of individual elements can taper off or become ill-advised at certain ratios (e.g., excessive brittleness from C or Cr3C2). Manufacturing homogeneity is challenging due to varying densities and melting points.. Future work: Future studies should focus on understanding tribo-oxidation behavior in different environmental conditions, creating guidelines for selecting solid lubricants, exploring additive manufacturing techniques (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) for HEA composites, and conducting detailed cost-performance matrix studies against conventional alloys.. Quote: "In general, HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC + BCC alloys."

W3046832734.title: Synthesis and Characterization of High Entropy Alloy and Coating

card: Paper card. Question: Can CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy coatings, produced via mechanical alloying and electro spark deposition, provide effective corrosion resistance and adhesion for stainless steel substrates in aggressive geothermal environments?. System: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy deposited on 316 L stainless steel substrate. Processing: Solid-state processing: Mechanical alloying of high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Mo powders for 30 h in a Pulverisette 6 Classic Line planetary ball mill (350 RPM, ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, N-Heptane process control agent) under Argon; cold pressing at 250 kN into 25 mm × 5 mm samples; sintering at 1100 °C for 1 h; machining into electrodes; electro spark deposition (ESD) under Argon atmosphere to deposit successive layers.. Test conditions: Pull-off testing per ASTM D4541–01; electrochemical corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 ± 0.5 °C for 6 h using potentiodynamic polarization.. Findings: Maximum adhesion resistance reached 0.67 MPa, limited by epoxy resin failure rather than coating-substrate interface failure.; Corrosion rate of the ESD coating calculated at 0.00016 mm/year in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.; Polarization resistance of the coating was higher than 316 L stainless steel (22.50 kΩ × cm2).; XRD analysis revealed an increase in σ phase (rich in Co, Cr, Fe) and μ phase (rich in Mo) in the coating compared to the sintered electrode.; The coating microstructure showed a homogeneous and adhesive layer near the substrate, with slight porosity and splats in the upper part.; After corrosion testing, a passivation layer formed on the surface, covering most pores, containing an oxygen component likely from segregated chromium.; The open circuit potential (Eoc) was more electronegative than the bulk as-cast alloy, attributed to increased porosity delaying passivation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the phase transformation (increase in σ and μ phases) to the rapid melting and cooling during the electro spark deposition process, driven by temperature differences and local solute solidification. The superior corrosion resistance is explained by the rapid formation of a passivation film, likely containing segregated chromium, which covers surface pores and reduces the corrosion current density significantly compared to bulk alloys or stainless steel.. Limitations: The coating is slightly porous in the upper part due to the BCC structure prone to pore formation in this high-entropy alloy and the ESD technique; the open circuit potential is more electronegative than the bulk alloy due to this porosity delaying passivation.. Future work: The authors state that novel promising coatings resistant to long-term high-temperature oxidation, corrosion action, and wear are currently being sought, implying further development is needed for these specific conditions.. card: Paper card. Question: What are the thermal stability, phase transition temperatures, and microstructural evolution of the metastable intermetallic phases in the CoCrFeMo0.85Ni high-entropy alloy?. System: CoCrFeMo0.85Ni high-entropy alloy (gas atomized powder, nominal equimolar CoCrFeNi with 0.85 Mo). Processing: Gas atomization of high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Mo, and Ni powders (approx. 24 µm); thermal analysis via DTA and DSC with 5 K/min heating/cooling cycles up to 1400 °C under Ar atmosphere; interrupted DTA at 900 °C; microstructural characterization via FEGSEM, EDX, and EBSD. Test conditions: Heating and cooling cycles at 5 K/min up to 1400 °C; interrupted heating at 900 °C; analysis of as-received powder, interrupted sample, and fully solidified sample. Findings: Solidus and liquidus temperatures determined as 1323 °C and 1331 °C, respectively.; Phase transitions observed at 800 °C (exothermal formation of intermetallics) and 1212 °C (endothermic dissolution).; As-received powder exhibits fine alternating layers suggesting spinodal-like morphology with minor elemental segregation.; After full thermal cycles, a dendritic microstructure forms with a single-phase FCC matrix.; The FCC matrix is depleted in Mo (<1/3 of dendrite content) and enriched in Ni compared to the dendrite core.; Dendrite cores contain a tetragonal (Co, Cr, Fe)-rich phase (presumed σ) surrounded by a Mo-rich rhombohedral phase (presumed µ).; The precipitation window for the cooling curve is identified between 780 °C and 1200 °C.; CALPHAD predictions show a single FCC phase above 1280 °C, which disagrees with DTA-derived liquidus at 1331 °C.. Mechanism: The formation of the FCC matrix is driven by high mixing entropy reducing Gibbs free energy. During solidification, Mo partitions to the liquid phase due to its high melting point and sluggish diffusion, segregating to interdendritic regions. The metastable phases (σ and µ) form via spinodal decomposition and compositional modulation driven by segregation, where Mo enrichment acts as a precursor state. The coexistence of σ and µ phases is attributed to cooperative diffusion and the order of elemental partitioning, with the µ phase growing at the periphery of the σ phase.. Limitations: The CALPHAD method may require further assessment for the transition temperatures of intermetallic formation in this HEA. The stabilization of the σ phase is a gradual process that is too slow to be fully observed in the DTA experiments due to kinetic effects. The study notes that the interaction of metastable phases in powder form can be eliminated by high-temperature treatment, limiting the observation of certain short-term phenomena.. Future work: Further detailed thermal analysis should be performed to derive remaining thermodynamic properties such as partial pressure and activity. Additional investigation of intermetallic phases is needed to facilitate understanding of atomic arrangement and orientation for optimal HEA design.. Quote: "Solidus and liquidus temperatures of CoCrFeMo0.85Ni were determined by differential thermal analysis as 1323 °C and 1331 °C, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: Does the equiatomic AlAgCuNiSnTi alloy meet the criteria for a high entropy alloy, and what are its microstructural, thermal, and corrosion properties?. System: AlAgCuNiSnTi equiatomic multicomponent alloy (six elements in equal atomic concentrations). Processing: Vacuum Arc Remelting (VAR) using MRF-ABJ900 equipment under argon atmosphere; five remelting cycles; samples also processed via melt spinning to obtain ~1 mm thick strips; homogenization heat treatment at 800 °C. Test conditions: Microhardness measured with FM-700 AHOTEC tester (HV0.1/15); thermal analysis via DTA and DIL at 10 °C/min heating/cooling rates; corrosion testing in 3.5% NaCl solution using potentiodynamic method with BioLogic SP-150. Findings: The alloy does not meet high entropy alloy criteria; ΔHmix = −10.13 kJ/mol and δ = 8.92 place it in the intermediate phase alloy range.; The as-cast microstructure is three-phase (four phases identified by XRD: TiNiSn, Ag3Sn, Al1.33Cu0.67, and Sn5Ti6).; Average microhardness of the as-cast alloy is 487 HV0.1/15, with the TiNi1.056Sn phase reaching a maximum of 600 HV0.1/15.; The corrosion rate stabilizes at 0.004 mm/y after initial passivation in 3.5% NaCl solution.; The corrosion rate (0.004 mm/y) is better than FeNiCoMnCrAl (0.009 mm/y) and FeNiCoMnCr (0.226 mm/y) HEAs in the same solution.; Homogenization at 800 °C did not cause major changes in the microstructure, though it slightly decreased hardness.; Melt spinning produced ~1 mm thick strips with a more homogeneous and grain-refined microstructure compared to the cast ingot.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the alloy forms intermediate phases rather than a single solid solution due to thermodynamic parameters (ΔHmix and δ) falling outside the high entropy alloy range. The high corrosion resistance is attributed to the positive action of titanium oxide forming a passivation layer on the surface.. Limitations: The alloy does not meet the criteria to be classified as a high entropy alloy; it contains multiple phases (intermetallics) rather than a single solid solution structure.. Future work: The authors propose that the alloy can be used for surface coating applications due to its high corrosion resistance.. Quote: "The results show that the as-cast alloy microstructure is three-phase, with an average microhardness of 487 HV0.1/15."

card: Paper card. Question: How do laser metal deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings perform regarding erosion and corrosion resistance in three distinct geothermal environments, and how do manufacturing defects influence their degradation?. System: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 (Mo-HEA) and Al0.5CoCrFeNi (Al-HEA) coatings deposited on carbon steel (S235JR) and stainless steel (AISI 316L, 304L) substrates. Processing: Laser metal deposition (LMD) using a Trumpf Trudisk 8002 5.3 kW disc laser system, Reis RV60-40 robot, and Oerlikon-Metco 10-C powder feeder under argon atmosphere; coating thickness 800–1000 µm; no post-deposition grinding or polishing. Test conditions: Three environments at Hellisheidi geothermal site: (1) Wellhead test at 194 °C and 14 bar (deaerated); (2) Aerated test at 90 °C and 1 bar (fluid mixed with atmospheric gas); (3) Erosion test at 198 °C and 15 bar (high-velocity fluid impact at 90° angle). Findings: Mo-HEA coatings on carbon steel exhibited manufacturing cracks up to 50–60 µm deep, while Mo-HEA on stainless steel showed no cracks.; Al-HEA coatings were prone to general and localized corrosion damage in all tests, forming oxide-rich films 20–40 µm thick in the wellhead test.; In the erosion test, Al-HEA coatings developed erosion pits deeper than 100 µm after a 90-day exposure period.; Erosion pits in Mo-HEA coatings were observed only at the location of pre-existing vertical cracks, where fluid turbulence increased damage.; Mo-HEA coatings on stainless steel substrates showed no adhesion damage or cracking in any of the three test environments.; Galvanic corrosion products (iron-based) formed at the interface of Mo-HEA coatings and carbon steel substrates after exposure and ambient drying.; The oxide layer on Mo-HEA in the aerated test was discontinuous, likely due to Cr concentration gradients and sluggish diffusion rates.. Mechanism: Manufacturing cracks in Mo-HEA on carbon steel induce fluid turbulence that accelerates erosion; Al-HEA suffers from internal stresses and rapid oxidation kinetics of Al leading to non-passive, brittle oxide films; galvanic effects between noble Mo-HEA and carbon steel exacerbate corrosion at interfaces upon exposure to ambient air.. Limitations: The study notes that surface roughness measurements were inconclusive due to scaling dominance, and the statistical null hypothesis method for erosion assessment failed due to high variability in coating thickness.. Future work: The formulation and production of the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating need to be optimized to prevent cracking on carbon steel substrates; longer exposure periods are needed to verify if the discontinuous oxide layer on Mo-HEA becomes continuous.. Quote: "Wide manufacturing cracks are concluded to enhance the fluid-induced erosion effect for the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating in the vicinity of the cracks."

card: Paper card. Question: How does a dual-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure in an equiatomic AlCrFeNiV high-entropy alloy influence its hardness and wear resistance under dry and lubricated sliding conditions?. System: Equiatomic AlCrFeNiV high-entropy alloy (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni, V). Processing: High-energy ball milling (SPEX 8000 mill, 2 h, ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, argon atmosphere) followed by spark plasma sintering (1100 °C for 1 h, 40 MPa axial pressure) and furnace cooling. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (5 N load, 15 s hold); reciprocating sliding wear against Al2O3 balls (10 N load, 0.18 m s−1 sliding speed, 30 min duration) under dry and lubricated (deionized water) conditions at ambient temperature. Findings: Hardness reached 1076 ± 15 HV0.5, significantly higher than previously reported values.; The microstructure consists of two BCC phases: BCC1 (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni) and BCC2 (enriched with 61.9 at.% V and Cr).; Average grain size was measured at 450 nm.; Wear rate under dry conditions was 17.2 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1.; Wear rate under lubricated conditions was 12.4 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1.; Average coefficient of friction (COF) was 0.34 in dry conditions and 0.15 under lubrication.; Hertzian contact stress at 10 N load was calculated to be 1887 MPa.; Oxygen content on the worn surface in dry friction was 2.2 at.% higher than in lubricated friction.. Mechanism: The superior hardness and wear resistance are attributed to solution strengthening from the mixture of two different BCC systems, high-density grain and phase boundaries acting as barriers to dislocation movement, and the inhibitory effect of the hard BCC2 phase on grain boundary movement and plastic flow. The wear mechanism involves abrasive wear, delamination, and oxidation, where a dense but locally unstable oxide layer forms and fractures, while the tight binding between BCC1 and BCC2 inhibits interfacial crack formation.. Limitations: The authors note that while hardness is very high, the plasticity of the alloy is poor, making the surface prone to fracture and generating fragments that can cause a secondary grinding effect and increase wear rates.. Future work: The authors suggest that the strategy of combining high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering is beneficial for developing new materials applicable in cutting tools.. Quote: "The hardness of the AlCrFeNiV alloys reached 1076 ± 15 HV0.5."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the weldability (specifically remelting behavior and susceptibility to hot/cold cracks) and wear resistance of a vanadium carbide-precipitating CrCoFeMoNiV high entropy alloy?. System: Cr27.5Co14Fe22Mo22Ni11.65V2.85 (atomic percent) high entropy alloy with intended vanadium carbide precipitation. Processing: Arc casting in a graphite crucible at approx. 1600 °C under argon atmosphere for 10 min with stirring; samples remelted on one side using TIG welding with 100 A current and 10 mm tip-to-workpiece distance. Test conditions: ASTM G75 Miller test for three-body abrasive wear (22.24 N load, 20 m/min speed, 6 hours duration, corundum F220 suspension); microstructural analysis via optical/SEM microscopy with Murakami etchant; Vickers hardness HV0.2. Findings: The as-cast alloy hardness is 324HV0.2, rising to 339HV0.2 after TIG remelting due to accelerated cooling.; No hot cracks, cold cracks, or pore formation were observed in the TIG remelted area.; The alloy exhibits a two-phase matrix (molybdenum-rich and molybdenum-poor/nickel-rich) with vanadium-chromium carbide and intermetallic precipitates.; Wear resistance (ablation 126 mm³) is comparable to Stellite 6 (122 mm³) and Stellite 12 (91 mm³) in the ASTM G75 test.; No distinct heat-affected zone (HAZ) was observed in the remelted microstructure.; EDX analysis showed a reduction of dissolved nickel by about 6 at.% and an increase in Cr and Mo content due to slag formation during casting.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the wear resistance to the precipitation of vanadium carbides and the high hardness of the matrix. The absence of a distinct HAZ and cracks is attributed to the alloy's basic remeltability, though the presence of a low-melting second phase in the interdendritic region theoretically increases the risk of hot cracking, which was not observed under the specific test conditions without external restraints.. Limitations: The study notes that EDX measurements have restrictions in accuracy regarding chemical composition determination. Additionally, the two-phase system with a low-melting phase creates a theoretical risk for hot cracking that was not fully validated under external stress conditions.. Future work: The authors propose adjusting the molybdenum content to achieve a single-phase system, increasing the carbon content to enhance carbide precipitation and wear resistance, and applying specific welding tests to determine cold cracking susceptibility.. Quote: "The hardness of the as cast alloy is 324HV0.2 and after remelting the hardness rises to 339HV0.2."

card: Paper card. Question: How does grain size influence the tribological behavior, wear mechanisms, and wear resistance of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloys under varying normal loads and sliding speeds?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) with fine grain (FG, ~2.9 μm) and coarse grain (CG, ~63.4 μm) microstructures. Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals followed by drop-casting into a copper mold, forging at 1000 °C, cold rolling (80% reduction), and annealing at 800 °C for 30 min (FG) or 1000 °C for 60 min (CG). Test conditions: Reciprocating sliding friction against a 10 mm Si3N4 ball under dry conditions at room temperature; normal loads of 5 N and 30 N; sliding speeds of 1, 5, and 10 mm/s; sliding time of 1200 s. Findings: The average grain size was 2.9 μm for the fine grain (FG) sample and 63.4 μm for the coarse grain (CG) sample.; The hardness of the FG sample was approximately 4.9 GPa, significantly higher than the CG sample's 3.4 GPa.; Under low load (5 N) and low speed (1 mm/s), the primary wear mechanism for both samples was adhesive wear.; With increased sliding speed, the wear mechanisms evolved to include adhesive wear and oxidation wear.; Under high load (30 N) and high speed, the wear mechanisms included adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation.; The specific wear rate of the FG sample was significantly lower than that of the CG sample across all tested conditions.; The oxide layer formed on the CG sample surface was prone to cracking and fracture, whereas the FG sample's oxide layer remained more intact.; Increasing the normal load from 5 N to 30 N resulted in a decrease in the friction coefficient due to the formation of a lubricating oxide layer.. Mechanism: The fine grain size provides higher surface strength and hardness, which improves wear resistance. Under friction heat, coarse grain samples soften more easily, causing their oxide layers to fracture and leading to increased wear. At high loads, the formation of a continuous oxide layer acts as a lubricant, reducing the friction coefficient, but the durability of this layer depends on the grain size and resulting hardness.. Quote: "The fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength."

card: Paper card. Question: How do cold spraying (CS) and high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying methods, combined with vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, 700 °C, and 900 °C, affect the microstructure, hardness, and corrosive wear properties of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings in simulated seawater drilling fluid?. System: CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings on 35CrMo steel substrate. Processing: Coatings prepared by cold spraying (CS) and high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying (HVOF) using hydrogen as fuel; followed by vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, 700 °C, and 900 °C for 2 h with a heating rate of 10 °C/min in a vacuum of <10⁻⁴ Pa. Test conditions: Friction and wear tests conducted in simulated seawater drilling fluid using a Φ6 silicon nitride ball, 10 N normal load, 5 Hz frequency, 1800 s duration, and 6 mm stroke. Findings: CoCrFeNiMn coatings prepared by CS and HVOF exhibit dense structures with porosity of approximately 1.1% and 1.4%, respectively, and bond well with the substrate.; Both CS and HVOF coatings achieve maximum microhardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, with values of 487.6 HV0.1 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively.; The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹) of the HVOF-500 °C coating.; Wear rates for both coating types at room temperature are very close, at 0.2952 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹ (CS) and 0.3016 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹ (HVOF).; Heat treatment at 700 °C and 900 °C causes a decrease in microhardness and an increase in wear rates due to grain coarsening and the formation of soft phases.; The HVOF coating exhibits higher porosity and more obvious peeling compared to the CS coating due to its layered thermal spray structure.; The wear mechanisms identified include adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear, and oxidation wear, with CS being mainly abrasive and HVOF showing more oxidative and adhesive wear.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the peak hardness and lowest wear rate at 500 °C to the formation of a heterogeneous structure with nanotwins in recrystallized grains and high-density dislocations. At higher temperatures (700–900 °C), complete recrystallization leads to grain coarsening and the formation of soft FCC matrix and B2 precipitates, reducing yield stress and hardness. Oxidation wear in HVOF coatings is exacerbated by the growth, rupture, and periodic peeling of oxide layers at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the HVOF coating has higher porosity and a layered structure leading to more peeling compared to CS.. Future work: The authors do not explicitly propose future work in the provided text.. Quote: "The two types of coatings achieve maximum hardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C; the Vickers microhardness of CS-500 °C and HVOF-500 °C are 487.6 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Hafnium (Hf) in varying amounts (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.42) to CoCrFeNi high entropy alloys affect the microstructure, phase composition, thickness, and diffusion mechanisms during boronizing and siliciding processes?. System: CoCrFeNiHfx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.42) high entropy alloys. Processing: Vacuum arc melting (2.1 × 10–6 mbar, 700 mbar Ar, 5 re-melts) followed by powder pack boronizing/siliciding using Ekabor II™ (90% SiC, 5% B4C, 5% KBF) at 1000 °C for 5 h in an electrical box furnace. Test conditions: Surface treatment at 1000 °C for 5 h; characterization via XRD (Cu-Kα, 20–80°, 1°/min), SEM, and EDS; cross-sectional analysis of samples cut in the middle. Findings: The combined thickness of the silicon-rich layer and boride layer (SL-1 + BL) decreased from 70 µm for CoCrFeNi to 63 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.1), 20 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.2), and 15 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.42).; The thickness of the transition/diffusion zone (DZ) increased with Hf content: 60 ± 4 µm (CoCrFeNi), 50 ± 3.5 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.1), 97 ± 9 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.2), and 126 ± 6 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.42).; XRD analysis identified the boride layer (BL) as containing Ni2Si, FeB, Fe2B, Co2B, and Cr5B3 phases.; In CoCrFeNi, Si atoms accumulated close to the BL but did not penetrate the substrate, whereas in CoCrFeNiHfx alloys, Si atoms penetrated through the Ni-rich Ni7Hf2 phase.; The microstructure transformed from single-phase FCC in CoCrFeNi to FCC + Ni7Hf2 (x=0.1) and finally to FCC + C15 Laves phases (x=0.42).; Cr-B rich precipitates (Cr5B3) were observed in the BL and DZ of CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNiHf0.1, but in CoCrFeNiHf0.2 and CoCrFeNiHf0.42, they were detected only in the DZ.; The eutectic structure in CoCrFeNiHf0.42 has lamellae with a distance of about 0.01 µm, which accelerates B diffusion.. Mechanism: Hf addition promotes the formation of Ni-Hf rich phases (Ni7Hf2 and C15 Laves) and fine eutectic structures; these phases act as channels for Si diffusion into the substrate, while the Cr-B rich layer at the interface hinders further Si transport. The fine eutectic microstructure in Hf-containing alloys accelerates B diffusion due to short diffusion distances and dominant grain/phase boundary diffusion, leading to a thicker diffusion zone but a thinner boride layer.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "Increasing the amount of Hf in the alloys resulted in a decrease in the combined layer thickness, which was measured for CoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiHf0.1, CoCrFeNiHf0.2, and CoCrFeNiHf0.42 to be 70 µm, 63 µm, 20 µm, and 15 µm, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a complex concentrated alloy be engineered to achieve ultralow wear rates across a wide temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) by utilizing nanohierarchical architecture and composition undulation?. System: Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 (at.%) complex concentrated alloy (designated NiX) and its counterpart Ni75(AlNbTiV)25 (designated Ni3X). Processing: Mechanical alloying (MA) followed by molding via spark plasma sintering (SPS). Test conditions: Sliding wear tests from room temperature to 800 °C; Vickers hardness and wear rate measurements; nanoindentation on worn tracks; SEM and TEM analysis of worn surfaces and subsurfaces. Findings: NiX achieved an ultralow wear rate in the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C, which is 1 to 3 orders of magnitude lower than comparative bulk alloys and steels.; At room temperature, NiX exhibited a wear rate of 1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm with a worn track depth of ~0.32 μm, effectively eliminating abrasive wear compared to Ni3X.; At 800 °C, NiX achieved a wear rate of 9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm, with the worn track depth being only one-tenth that of Ni3X due to a dense, fully covering glaze layer.; The NiX matrix contains nano-coupled equiaxed grains (average size 176 nm) with hierarchical A2 nanoprecipitates (average diameter 20 nm) and composition undulations where Ni fluctuates by up to 63%.; Nanoindentation revealed that the H/E and H3/E2 ratios on the worn surface of NiX at room temperature (0.0548 and 0.0276) were significantly higher than those of Ni3X (0.0306 and 0.0054).; The subsurface of worn NiX evolved into a gradient structure with a nanocrystalline tribo-layer (~500 nm deep) and an ultra-fine grained tribo-layer (~1.5 μm deep), unlike the bimodal structure of Ni3X.; Dislocation densities in the NiX subsurface decreased with depth: 2.7 × 10^11 mm−2 in the NC layer, 6.4 × 10^10 mm−2 in the UFG layer, and 3.0 × 10^9 mm−2 at the bottom of the UFG layer.; At 800 °C, the oxygen concentration on the entire worn surface of NiX exceeded 35 at.%, forming a continuous glaze layer with a hardness of ~7.0 GPa.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation enables adaptive friction interface protection through multiple depth-dependent deformation pathways. At room temperature, the coexistence of A1 to A3 nano-coupled grains and A2 nanoprecipitates activates geometrically necessary dislocations, stacking faults (SFs), and deformation twins (DTs) to create a gradient recrystallized tribo-layer that releases frictional stress progressively and prevents strain localization. At high temperatures (≥600 °C), the high concentration of oxidation-prone elements facilitates the rapid formation of a dense, protective nanocrystalline glaze layer that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear, while the heterostructure suppresses grain coarsening.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the specific origin of the nanohierarchical architecture formation requires more detailed simulations and experiments to confirm.. Future work: The authors propose that the work provides guidance for fabricating ultra-wear-resistant alloys by exploiting multicomponent heterostructures, and suggest that the formation mechanism of the nanohierarchical architecture requires more detailed simulations and experiments to confirm.. Quote: "yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C"

Paper card. Question: How do nanohierarchical architecture and composition undulation in complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) influence high-temperature wear resistance and the formation of protective oxide layers?. System: Ni3X and NiX complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) based on Ni, Al, Nb, Ti, and V elements. Processing: High-energy ball milling (300 r/min, 32 h, 5:1 ball-to-powder ratio, argon atmosphere) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1,050 °C for 8 min under 35 MPa pressure. Test conditions: Ball-on-disc tribometer, Si3N4 counterbody (Ø 6 mm), normal load 5 N, sliding speed 0.2 m/s, sliding distance 360 m, temperature range RT to 800 °C. Findings: The Ni3X alloy forms a loose oxide layer with an outer columnar crystal (diameter ~120 nm, thickness ~317 nm) and an internal nanocrystal layer (thickness ~475 nm) at 800 °C, leading to high wear.; The NiX alloy forms a dense glaze layer with an average thickness of 393 nm at 800 °C, resulting in ultra-low wear rates.; In Ni3X, the outer oxide layer consists of NiO columnar crystals, while the internal layer contains Nb2O5, TiO2, and V2O5 nanocrystals, with visible gaps causing delamination.; In NiX, the glaze layer is enriched in Nb, Ti, and V elements and comprises nanocrystalline metallic oxides including Nb2O5, TiO2, V2O5, and NiO.; Discontinuous (Al, O)-rich nanoparticles with an average grain size of 64 nm form in the subsurface of Ni3X, whereas larger nanoparticles (175 nm) form in NiX.; The deformed tribo-layer of NiX containing alumina nanoparticles and amorphous oxides exhibits higher hardness (7.6 GPa) and elastic modulus (179 GPa) compared to the undeformed substrate (7.0 GPa and 134 GPa).; Grain coarsening in the subsurface of Ni3X increases average grain size to ~340 nm (A1) and ~152 nm (A3) within a depth of 1 μm to 3.5 μm, degrading wear resistance.; The average grain size of A1 to A3 nano-coupled grains in the worn subsurface of NiX is ~195 nm, indicating good thermal stability compared to the as-fabricated state.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high Ni concentration in Ni3X leads to preferential formation of NiO, which acts as a high-valent dopant increasing vacancy concentration and micro-voids, creating a loose, non-protective oxide layer prone to spallation. In contrast, NiX's balanced composition facilitates the formation of a dense, protective glaze layer rich in Nb, Ti, and V oxides. This glaze layer, combined with in-situ formed Al2O3 nanoparticles and amorphous oxides, creates a nanocomposite tribo-layer that enhances deformability, inhibits grain coarsening via solute-drag and energy dissipation, and prevents delamination.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the specific wear response is observed in the current CCA system and suggests applicability to other systems.. Future work: The authors propose that the wear response found in the current CCA can be selectively applicable to other alloy systems to achieve pleasing wear resistance.. Quote: "The loose oxide layer increases the wear of the Ni3X, while the dense glaze layer imparts ultra-low wear to the NiX."

card: Paper card. Question: How can atomic-level complexity in complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) be quantitatively engineered to predict and maximize solid-solution strengthening without relying on computationally expensive electronic structure calculations for every new composition?. System: 3d transition metal CCAs (V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) and a specific binary NiV solid solution (63.2 at.% Ni, 36.8 at.% V). Processing: Arc melting of 99.9% purity ingredients under Ti-gettered Argon; suction casting into water-cooled copper molds; homogenization at 1050–1200 °C for 24 h; cold rolling (70–85% reduction); recrystallization annealing in Ar followed by water quenching; for NiV specifically: cold rolling to 30% reduction, homogenization at 1075 °C for 45 h, cold rolling to 60% reduction, and annealing at 920 °C for 3 min.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature with an engineering strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1; grain size of the NiV sample was 8.1 µm; comparison alloys (CrCoNi, CrMnFeCoNi) had similar grain sizes.. Findings: The yield strength of the binary NiV solid solution is approximately 750 MPa, which is nearly double that of the Cantor high-entropy alloy (CrMnFeCoNi).; Solid-solution strengthening (σSS) in 3d CCAs is proportional to the configurational fluctuation of atomic-level pressure (ΔPsolute), with a correlation coefficient indicating a clear proportional relationship.; The atomic-level pressure in 3d CCAs is driven primarily by charge transfer (dQ) rather than atomic size difference, as the order of pressure (Cr<Mn<Fe<Co<Ni) is opposite to the order of pure atomic sizes.; The macroscopic difference in charge transfer among elements (Δelement(dQ)) is approximately 2.0 to 2.4 times larger than the average configurational difference within elements, allowing prediction of local fluctuations from elemental averages.; Solid-solution strengthening can be rationalized and predicted using the electronegativity difference (Δχ) among constituent elements, where NiV has a Δχ of 0.169 compared to 0.080 for CrMnFeCoNi.; Mixing entropy (ΔSmix) is not strongly correlated with solid-solution strengthening; alloys with lower mixing entropy (like binary NiV) can exhibit higher strength if they have a large electronegativity difference.; The ultimate tensile strength of the developed NiV alloy is close to 1200 MPa.. Mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening originates from the configurational fluctuation of atomic-level pressure, which arises from charge transfer between neighboring elements. This charge transfer creates local electronic energy variations that interact with the elastic field of dislocations. The magnitude of this fluctuation can be approximated by the electronegativity difference among the constituent elements, which serves as a proxy for the average charge transfer and its variance.. Limitations: The prediction of solid-solution strength does not account for other micromechanical strengthening mechanisms such as grain boundary strengthening, which contributed 2/3 of the yield strength in CrMnFeCoNi. The study assumes random chemical mixtures, though short-range order may exist and could be favored in alloys with high Δχ.. Future work: Further studies are required to explore quantitative relationships between atomic-level pressure, charge transfer, and various deformation mechanisms including grain boundary strengthening and thermal activation barriers. The authors suggest that charge transfer may also dominate lattice strain energy and phase stability, warranting further investigation into these electronic-to-macro couplings.. Quote: "This approach can be used for designing alloys with customized properties, such as a simple binary NiV solid solution whose yield strength exceeds that of the Cantor high-entropy alloy by nearly a factor of two."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the plastic deformation mechanisms at the micro/nanoscale of graphene oxide-reinforced high-entropy alloy composites, and how do they differ from pure HEA?. System: Fe22Co24Cr20Ni23Al11 HEA matrix reinforced with 0.0, 0.3, 0.6, and 1.0 wt.% Graphene Oxide (GO). Processing: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 900°C for 5 min under 45 MPa pressure and 10 Pa vacuum; micropillars (3 μm diameter, aspect ratio 2) fabricated via FIB with [001] orientation; MD simulations using LAMMPS with 1 fs time step and 12 m/s compression rate.. Test conditions: Micropillar compression to 0.30 strain at 2 × 10−3 s−1 strain rate; MD nanopillar compression (12 nm diameter) under NVT ensemble at 300 K.. Findings: Hardness increased with GO content up to 0.6 wt.% (7.09 GPa for A3) then decreased to 6.31 GPa for 1.0 wt.% (A4).; Yield strength and flow stress of composites were higher than pure HEA, peaking at 0.6 wt.% GO.; Pure HEA micropillars showed localized deformation with single slip traces, while 0.6 wt.% GO composites exhibited homogeneous deformation.; MD simulations revealed only mobile 1/2 <111> perfect dislocations in pure HEA, whereas composites contained immobile <100> interstitial dislocations.; GO sheets effectively impeded dislocation movement, causing dislocation congestion above the sheet in composites.; Composites with 1.0 wt.% GO showed reduced strengthening due to GO sheet aggregation and Cr carbide segregation at grain boundaries.; The yield strength of composites climbed and then declined with increasing GO content, with the maximum at 0.6 wt.%.. Mechanism: Strengthening is attributed to grain refinement (pinning effect of GO sheets) and the formation of immobile <100> interstitial dislocations via reaction of 1/2 <111> perfect dislocations on {110} planes. These immobile dislocations pin mobile dislocations and restrict their motion, requiring higher stress to activate deformation sources. Additionally, GO sheets physically block dislocation propagation, limiting plastic deformation to the upper region of the nanopillar.. Limitations: The text states that the essential cause of the reduced strengthening efficiency in the 1.0 wt.% sample was initially unrevealed, though later attributed to agglomeration and segregation. It also notes that the HEA sample used has a substantial BCC structure which results in weaker plastic deformation compared to FCC structures, potentially limiting the observation of stress bursts.. Quote: "The immobile <100> interstitial dislocations also participated in the plastic deformation of composites, in contrast to pure HEA counterpart where only mobile 1/2 <111> perfect dislocations dominated deformation."

card: Paper card. Question: How do surface conditions (clean vs. oxidized/passivated) influence the deformation mechanisms and mechanical behaviors of lead (Pb) nanocrystals?. System: Pb nanoparticles (diameters < 25 nm) and surface-passivated Pb particles with PbOx layers. Processing: In situ heat treatment of PX-PbTiO3 nanowires at 350°C under electron beam irradiation (beam density ~4×10^4 A/m^2) to form Pb particles; surface passivation achieved by prolonged electron beam irradiation (~10 minutes) to form PbOx layers; mechanical testing using electrochemically etched W tips (2.5 V, 20 mA NaOH etching) at ~0.3 nm/s inside an aberration-corrected FEI Titan 80-300 TEM. Test conditions: In situ mechanical compression and stretching inside an aberration-corrected TEM at room temperature (implied by lack of heating during test), with particle sizes ranging from ~11.7 nm to 16.7 nm. Findings: 78% of clean Pb particles exhibited dominant diffusive pseudoelastic deformation, while only 22% showed displacive plasticity.; 100% of surface-passivated Pb particles demonstrated displacive plastic deformation with no pseudoelasticity.; A threshold particle diameter of 67 nm was derived below which diffusive deformation overwhelms displacive deformation in pure Pb.; Clean Pb particles recovered their initial ellipsoid shape after compression and stretching due to surface atom diffusion.; Surface-passivated Pb particles retained irregular shapes after unloading due to suppressed diffusion and dominant plasticity.; Twinning and stacking fault formation were more favored in surface-passivated particles compared to clean particles.; Surface passivation increased the stress required to drive plastic deformation, as seen in half-passivated particles where the clean segment stretched while the passivated segment remained stable.. Mechanism: In clean Pb nanoparticles, surface atom diffusion dominates and drives pseudoelastic deformation by minimizing surface energy. In surface-passivated particles, the PbOx layer inhibits surface diffusion, forcing deformation to proceed via displacive mechanisms such as dislocation slip, stacking faults, and twinning, which result in irreversible plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study focuses specifically on Pb; the authors note that the surface condition effect is expected to be most prominent in active metals with small sizes and good surface diffusivities (e.g., Cu, Bi, Sn, Ag), implying generalizability to other metals requires further verification.. Future work: The authors propose that surface engineering can be used to tune the mechanical properties of small-volume metals and suggest investigating the surface condition effect in other active metals like Cu, Bi, Sn, and Ag.. Quote: "In most of the pristine Pb particles, surface atom diffusion dominates and leads to a pseudoelastic deformation behavior."

card: Paper card. Question: Can machine learning reliably predict the crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC, MIP) of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) synthesized via melting and casting routes without using synthetic data augmentation, and is synthetic data augmentation a reliable practice for this domain?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 30 elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mn, Ti, V, Nb, Mo, Zr, Hf, Ta, W, C, Mg, Zn, Si, Re, N, Li, Sn, Be, B, Ag, Pt, Y, Pd, Au); specifically a novel alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25.. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of elemental buttons (Ni, Cu, Fe, Co, Al; purity > 99.99%) under high purity Ar environment, followed by multiple melting/solidification cycles for homogeneity, vacuum sealing in quartz tube, homogenization at 1000 °C for 10 h, and water quenching.. Test conditions: Machine learning models trained on 1200 experimental datasets from melting/casting routes; tested on 240 samples from original data and 279 samples from augmented data (1200 original + 192 synthetic); XRD analysis performed with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) at 20°–100° (2θ).. Findings: The vanilla Random Forest Classifier (V-RFC) achieved the highest performance with an average test accuracy of 84%, ROC-AUC score of 0.9649, and tenfold cross-validation mean score of 0.9315.; Synthetic data augmentation using SMOTE-Tomek links increased average test accuracy to 92% (1392 datasets) but did not yield significant breakthroughs in correct/incorrect phase predictions compared to the original dataset.; The V-RFC model correctly predicted the FCC phase for the newly synthesized alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25, which was confirmed by XRD showing Bragg's peaks (111), (200), (220), (311), and (222).; Five physical parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) were identified as crucial for phase prediction, with no strong multicollinearity observed between them.; The model was limited in interpreting the exact number and types of phases in complex multiphase HEAs, often classifying them broadly as MIP (Mixture of Intermetallic Phases).; Hyper-parameter tuning of the RFC model (HT-RFC) resulted in an approximate 3% increment in average test accuracy to 87.49%.; The study found that mixing data from different synthesis routes causes spurious effects, justifying the exclusion of non-melting/casting routes from the dataset.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the Random Forest Classifier's ensemble of decision trees effectively handles the imbalanced dataset of experimental data without the need for synthetic augmentation, which they claim introduces uncertainty regarding whether generated samples are truly high-entropy alloys. The model relies on the correlation of five thermodynamic and geometric parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) to distinguish between solid-solution phases (FCC, BCC) and intermetallic mixtures (MIP).. Limitations: The method is limited in exactly interpreting the number and types of phases present in a complex multiphase HEA, as it typically predicts such cases as a single 'MIP' category rather than resolving specific phase combinations.. Future work: A follow-on work will test and predict the mechanical properties of HEAs, which will require atomistic studies using Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with EAM potentials for 16 elements (Cu, Ag, Au, Ni, Pd, Pt, Al, Pb, Fe, Mo, Ta, W, Mg, Co, Ti, Zr).. Quote: "We found that (i) RFC model predictions were more reliable in contrast to other models and (ii) the synthetic data augmentation is not a neat practice in materials science specially to develop HEAs, where it cannot assure phase information reliably."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the compiled mechanical properties of high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) be used to assess their potential as structural materials and guide future development?. System: 370 high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), including 3d transition metal, refractory metal (RHEAs and RCCAs), light metal family, and bronzes and brasses HEAs/CCAs families; HEAs defined as alloys with 5 or more principal elements (5-35 at%); CCAs defined as alloys with 3 or more principal components.. Processing: Compilation of data from published reports from 2004 to 2016; density estimated using rule of mixtures (ROM): ρ=∑xiMi/∑xiVi; Young's modulus estimated using ROM for single phase solid solutions only: E=∑xiEi.. Test conditions: Uniaxial loading (tension or compression) at room temperature for 370 alloys; temperature-dependent testing for 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs).. Findings: The database covers mechanical properties for 370 HEAs and CCAs reported between 2004 and 2016.; For 27 refractory HEAs, yield stress and elongation are provided as a function of testing temperature.; The database includes alloy composition, microstructure type, density, hardness, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength, and Young's modulus.; Data entries are organized in a tree-like classification with four families and expanded into classes based on principal element combinations.; The database enables users to browse, search, filter, and plot material property maps using performance indices defined by M. F. Ashby.. Mechanism: The authors explain that HEAs are presumably stabilized by the configurational entropy of mixing, while CCAs encompass a broader range of alloys with single-phase or multi-phase microstructures; the database allows for the evaluation of performance indices for lighter, stronger, and stiffer structures.. Limitations: The properties are not equally populated for every alloy due to the lack of literature data.. Future work: The database can be used to represent various property spaces, calculate performance indices, and enable data mining to extract insights and uncover patterns to guide and accelerate the development of HEAs and CCAs.. Quote: "The database covers the main mechanical properties of HEAs and CCAs tested under uniaxial loading from published reports since 2004 until end of 2016."
