Question: How can decision tree methodology be applied to establish classification systems based on multiple covariates or develop prediction algorithms for a target variable, specifically regarding variable selection, handling missing values, and managing skewed data?. Findings: Decision tree algorithms (CART, C4.5, CHAID, QUEST) are non-parametric and can efficiently deal with large, complicated datasets without imposing a complicated parametric structure.; In a cohort study of major depressive disorder, individuals were divided into 28 subgroups where the risk of the disorder varied from 0 to 38%.; Specific high-risk subgroup identified: 17.2% of male smokers with a Goldberg depression scale score of 2 or 3 and no full-time job had MDD at the 4-year follow-up.; Low-risk subgroup identified: Only 2% of non-smokers at baseline had MDD four years later.; Variable importance is computed based on the reduction of model accuracy or the purities of nodes when a variable is removed.; Stopping rules parameters include the minimum number of records in a leaf, the minimum number of records in a node prior to splitting, and the depth of any leaf from the root node.. Mechanism: The algorithm classifies a population into branch-like segments that construct an inverted tree with a root node, internal nodes, and leaf nodes. It splits parent nodes into purer child nodes based on input variables related to the target, using characteristics like entropy, Gini index, or information gain to choose splits. The process continues until pre-determined homogeneity or stopping criteria are met, or a large tree is grown and then pruned to optimal size to prevent overfitting.. Limitations: The main disadvantage is that it can be subject to overfitting and underfitting, particularly when using a small data set, which limits generalizability. Strong correlation between input variables may result in selecting variables that improve model statistics but are not causally related to the outcome.. Future work: Further applications include developing methods for survival prediction endpoints, selecting input variables based on relative cost or clinical meaningfulness rather than just statistical properties, and creating trees to identify subgroups of patients for different diagnostic tests or treatment strategies.. Quote: "This method classifies a population into branch-like segments that construct an inverted tree with a root node, internal nodes, and leaf nodes."

W3112329799.title: Expanded dataset of mechanical properties and observed phases of multi-principal element alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How to systematically document experimentally reported high-entropy alloy microstructures and metallurgy-specific features to support machine learning-based phase classification?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 1362 multicomponent alloys selected through the end of August 2020, excluding glassy, amorphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases. Processing: Synthesis routes, hot- or cold-working, homogenization (temperature and time), annealing (temperature and time), and quenching were extracted from peer-reviewed experimental articles. Test conditions: Data derived from experimental peer-reviewed research articles; no new experimental testing was performed in this data article. Findings: The dataset contains 1422 entries with seventeen columns covering identification, composition, empirical parameters, processing, and microstructure; The final dataset includes 1362 multicomponent alloys after removing entries with missing data and eliminating glassy, amorphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases; Microstructural phases are categorized as single solid solution (FCC, BCC), dual-phase (FCC+BCC), or other intermetallic/laves/martensitic phases (Im); Empirical design parameters calculated include density estimate, enthalpy of mixing (dHmix), entropy of mixing (dSmix), melting temperature (Tm), valence electron concentration (VEC), atomic size difference (δ), and difference in Pauling negativities (χ); Visualization shows that solid solution phases are particularly more sensitive to empirical parameters than intermetallic (IM) phases. Mechanism: The authors explain that the dataset serves as a systematic documentation to enable machine learning and material informatics methods to extract insights and trends not immediately available from individual studies. Limitations: The article is limited to typical empirical parameters for succinctness, though others can be developed from alloy specifications. Future work: Different machine learning and material informatics computational methods can be applied to this dataset to extract insights and trends thereby advancing the real-world applications of these alloys. Quote: "After removing entries missing some data and eliminating glassy, amourphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases, the as-constructed dataset is reduced to 1362 multicomponent alloys."

W2969084129.title: Diffusion barrier with 30-fold improved performance using AlCrTaTiZrN high-entropy alloy

card: Paper card. Question: How do grain size, melting behavior, elastic properties, and deformation mechanisms change in nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys?. System: CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition). Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS software; models built via Voronoi construction with average grain sizes of 3.6, 3.0, 2.5, and 2.0 nm; equilibrated in Nose-Hoover NPT ensemble at 0 GPa and 300 K; tensile strain applied at 0.05%/ps in x-direction with NPT in y and z directions.. Test conditions: Temperature range 300–3000 K for melting; uniaxial tensile strain at 300 K with strain rates up to 5 × 10^8/s; strain levels up to 40% for stress-strain analysis.. Findings: Melting point decreases from 1940 K (single crystal) to 1430 K (3.6 nm grain size), 1340 K (2.5 nm), and is obscured by amorphization at 2.0 nm.; Shear modulus reduces by 22% and Young's modulus by 20% as grain size decreases from 3.6 nm to 2.0 nm.; Ultimate tensile strength decreases from 3.4 GPa (3.6 nm) to 3.0 GPa (2.5 nm), with the 2.0 nm sample showing a peak at 5% strain due to amorphization.; FCC composition drops from 60% (3.6 nm) to 19% (2.0 nm) at 0% strain, indicating severe amorphization at the smallest grain size.; Inverse Hall-Petch relation observed: flow stress increases with grain size (d) according to the fitted linear equation.; Plastic deformation increases with decreasing grain size for samples >2.0 nm, but decreases at 2.0 nm due to amorphization.; Diffusion coefficient of Mn is highest among all elements in the molten state at 3000 K, with an average value of 15.0 × 10⁻⁹ m²·s⁻¹.. Mechanism: At the nanoscale, plastic deformation is governed by grain-boundary mediated processes rather than dislocation motion. The primary mechanisms include grain shape change, stacking fault formation, and amorphization, which become dominant as grain size decreases to 2.0 nm, leading to a reduction in plasticity despite the general trend of increased ductility in larger nanocrystalline samples.. Limitations: The text notes deviations between theoretical and experimental values due to the complex composition of the alloy and varying experimental conditions; it also states that the amorphization at 2.0 nm makes observing volume changes during melting difficult.. Quote: "The stress-strain simulation demonstrates that the ultimate tensile strength decreases with the decrease of the grain size, while the plastic deformation increases with the decrease in grain size."

Question: How does phase separation (specifically Cu-rich grain boundaries and Cu-rich grains) affect the mechanical properties and nanoscale deformation mechanisms of the Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy under uniaxial tensile loading?. System: Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition with Cu-rich regions up to 80% Cu content). Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using LAMMPS code with Farkas et al. interatomic potential; models constructed as 2D sheets (60 × 60 × 3.62 nm³, 1,098,730 atoms) and 3D cubes (23.4 nm side, 1,080,458 atoms); equilibration via energy minimization, 2 ns relaxation at 5 GPa/300 K, and 2 ns relaxation at 0 GPa/300 K; uniaxial tensile deformation applied at 300 K with a strain rate of 4.0 × 10⁷ s⁻¹. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile loading along the X-direction at 300 K; strain rate of 4.0 × 10⁷ s⁻¹; periodic boundary conditions in all three directions; analysis via adaptive common-neighbor analysis (CNA) and atomic strain modifiers. Findings: Cu-rich grain boundaries significantly reduced ductility, causing intergranular fracture at 7.4% strain in 2D samples and 7.8% strain in 3D samples.; The yield strength of samples with Cu-rich grain boundaries was lower than random composition distribution (RCD) samples.; Cu-rich grains lowered the overall strength of the alloy, with the strength decrease becoming more obvious as the volume fraction of Cu-rich grains increased.; The critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) of Cu-depleted grains was greater than that of Cu-rich grains, meaning slip systems in Cu-rich grains activated first.; Dislocation slipping and grain boundary sliding were identified as the main mechanisms of plastic deformation.; The internal slip system was predominantly of the <112>{111} type rather than the common <110>{111} type due to lattice distortion and energy considerations.; An uneven stress distribution was observed where the stress on Cu-depleted grains was much higher than that on Cu-rich grains.. Mechanism: Phase separation creates regions with different mechanical properties; Cu-rich regions have lower strength and lower critical resolved shear stress, causing plastic deformation to initiate there first. In Cu-rich grain boundary samples, the low strength of the boundaries leads to early cracking and intergranular fracture, reducing ductility. In Cu-rich grain samples, the lower CRSS of Cu-rich grains causes them to yield first, lowering the macroscopic strength, while the stress concentration in Cu-depleted grains can sometimes override this if the stress distribution is uneven.. Limitations: The simulations used a relatively high loading rate of 4.0 × 10⁷ s⁻¹ due to timescale limitations of MD, ideal crystal structures, and extreme purity, leading to considerably higher yield stress compared to conventional experiments.. Future work: The theoretical investigation of phase separation influence on deformation behaviors may inspire new ideas to improve the mechanical properties of the alloy and expand its practical application.. Quote: "Cu-rich grain boundaries significantly reduced ductility."
